name: Frog Traveler
description: Frog Gorf is traveling through Swamp kingdom. Unfortunately, after a poor jump, he fell into a well of $$$n$$$ meters depth. Now Gorf is on the bottom of the well and has a long way up. The surface of the well's walls vary in quality: somewhere they are slippery, but somewhere have convenient ledges. In other words, if Gorf is on $$$x$$$ meters below ground level, then in one jump he can go up on any integer distance from $$$0$$$ to $$$a_x$$$ meters inclusive. (Note that Gorf can't jump down, only up). Unfortunately, Gorf has to take a break after each jump (including jump on $$$0$$$ meters). And after jumping up to position $$$x$$$ meters below ground level, he'll slip exactly $$$b_x$$$ meters down while resting. Calculate the minimum number of jumps Gorf needs to reach ground level.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 300\,000$$$) — the depth of the well. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le i$$$), where $$$a_i$$$ is the maximum height Gorf can jump from $$$i$$$ meters below ground level. The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$ ($$$0 \le b_i \le n - i$$$), where $$$b_i$$$ is the distance Gorf will slip down if he takes a break on $$$i$$$ meters below ground level.
output_specification: If Gorf can't reach ground level, print $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, firstly print integer $$$k$$$ — the minimum possible number of jumps. Then print the sequence $$$d_1,\,d_2,\,\ldots,\,d_k$$$ where $$$d_j$$$ is the depth Gorf'll reach after the $$$j$$$-th jump, but before he'll slip down during the break. Ground level is equal to $$$0$$$. If there are multiple answers, print any of them.
approach_summary: Exploit monotonicity of two-pointer invariant [L, R]. Advance R while shifting L forward to maintain validity, running in O(N) amortized time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1601B — Frog Traveler [34. Two Pointers]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: When scanning contiguous subarrays or paired indices, advancing the right pointer $R$ monotonically tightens or relaxes the constraint, allowing the left pointer $L$ to only advance forward without ever needing to reset backwards.
